why_how.text: Lane lines tell you which way traffic moves and when you may cross.
Passing has firm distance rules and places where it is illegal.

scenario.text: A driver on a two-lane road wants to pass a slow truck one hundred feet before a railroad crossing.

reasoning.text: Passing is illegal within one hundred feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct or a tunnel.

result.text: The driver stays behind the truck until well past the crossing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a solid yellow line may be crossed to pass whenever the road looks clear.

correction.text: A broken yellow line may be crossed to pass once the way is safe, while a solid yellow line should be crossed only to turn.

memory_support.text: Yellow splits directions, white splits lanes; one lane at a time.

prompt.text: After passing a car on a two-lane road, how far ahead of an oncoming vehicle must you be back on the right?

rationale.text: Make sure the passing lane is clear, because you must be back on the right at least one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on safe vehicle operation. In this lesson you will learn what yellow and white lane lines tell you, which lane slower traffic should use, how to change lanes one step at a time, how to pass another vehicle and return to your lane, where passing is illegal, and what to do when someone is passing you. The manual gives exact distances for passing, so pay attention to the one-hundred-foot rules that appear twice in this lesson. Keep this in mind as you practice. Read each practice question carefully.

Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions. A broken yellow line may be crossed to pass once the way is safe, while a solid yellow line should be crossed only to turn. White lines divide lanes moving the same direction. You may cross a broken white line to change lanes when safe, but you should not cross a solid white line. On the highway, slower vehicles should keep right, leaving the left lane for faster or passing traffic. So the color tells you the direction of the traffic beside you, and the broken or solid pattern tells you whether you may cross.

lines.text: One lane at a time, with a signal.

narration.text: Change only one lane at a time, and give a proper signal before any turn or lane change. Before changing lanes, check the lane ahead, check your mirrors for anyone about to pass you, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, signal, then move over smoothly. Weaving in and out of lanes greatly raises the risk of a crash. So a lane change is a short sequence of checks followed by a signal and a smooth move, done one lane at a time, and it is never a series of quick moves from lane to lane through traffic. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Back on the right one hundred feet early.
Return when you see it in the mirror.
Being passed: do not speed up.

narration.text: Before passing, make sure the passing lane is clear, because you must be back on the right side of the road at least one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle. Stay in the passing lane until the vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror, then signal before moving back. When another vehicle is passing you on the left, let it pass safely and do not speed up. So passing needs a clear lane and room to return, and being passed needs you to hold your speed and let the other driver complete the pass. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Solid yellow on your side; no-passing signs.
Within one hundred feet of crossings.

narration.text: Passing is illegal where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, where a No Passing Zone pennant or a Do Not Pass sign is posted, on or near a curve, and near the crest of a hill. Passing is also illegal within one hundred feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct or a tunnel. So there are two kinds of bans: those shown by markings, signs, curves and hills, and those set by distance from places such as intersections and crossings. Check for both before you decide to pass. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Trap: a clear road means passing is fine.
Solid yellow: cross only to turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When the road ahead looks empty, a driver may feel free to cross a solid yellow line to pass. The manual says a solid yellow line should be crossed only to turn, and passing is illegal where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line. A broken yellow line is the one that may be crossed to pass once the way is safe. A second trap is distance. Passing is illegal within one hundred feet of an intersection, railroad crossing, bridge, viaduct or tunnel, even where the line is broken. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: How early must you be back?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are passing a car on a two-lane road. How far ahead of an oncoming vehicle must you be back on the right side? Recall the passing rule. Before passing, make sure the passing lane is clear, because you must be back on the right side of the road at least one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle. So the answer is at least one hundred feet. Stay in the passing lane until the passed car shows in your rearview mirror, then signal before you move back. If you guessed a shorter distance, review this rule.

Let us wrap up. Yellow lines divide opposite directions and white lines divide the same direction, broken lines may be crossed when safe, a solid yellow only to turn, and a solid white not at all. Slower vehicles keep right. Change one lane at a time with checks and a signal, and avoid weaving. When passing, be back on the right one hundred feet before oncoming traffic and return once the car shows in your mirror. Do not pass on a solid yellow, near signs, curves or crests, or within one hundred feet of crossings, and when being passed, do not speed up.

why_how.text: Turning from the right lane with the right signal keeps other drivers informed and out of your path.
All-way stops and roundabouts have set rules for who goes first.

scenario.text: You and another driver reach an all-way stop at the same time, and the other driver is on your right.

reasoning.text: At an all-way stop the first vehicle to stop goes first, and when two arrive together the vehicle on the left yields.

result.text: You are the vehicle on the left, so you yield and let the other driver go first.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a roundabout and a traffic circle work the same way.

correction.text: A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, while a traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs.

memory_support.text: First stopped goes first; roundabouts run counterclockwise and entering yields.

prompt.text: You are entering a roundabout and cars are already circulating. Who yields?

answer.text: You do. Entering traffic always yields to traffic already circulating.

rationale.text: Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise, enters and leaves by right turns, and entering traffic yields.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on turns and intersections. In this lesson you will learn which lane to use for each turn, which signals are safest, how center left-turn lanes are used and marked, where U-turns are banned and how a median U-turn intersection works, what to do when the driver ahead slows to turn, who goes first at an all-way stop, and how traffic moves and yields in a roundabout, including roundabouts with more than one lane and large vehicles inside them. Keep this in mind as you practice. Read each practice question carefully.

To turn left, get into the far-left lane for your direction well ahead of the turn, and to turn right use the far-right lane, signaling and yielding to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians. Built-in lighted turn signals are the safest signal. Hand signals may be used if a lighted signal fails, but not on a driving skills exam. When the driver ahead signals a turn or slows as if to turn, slow down and be ready to stop. So plan the lane early, signal with your lights, and give room to the turning driver ahead of you. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Never pass in a center left-turn lane.
No U-turns on curves, crests, interstates.

narration.text: Never use a center left-turn lane to pass, and watch for oncoming drivers entering it to turn left in front of you. Center lanes reserved for left turns are usually marked with CENTER LANE ONLY signs or pavement arrows, though some have neither. Never make a U-turn on a curve, near the crest of a hill, or on an interstate, where you should go to the next exit and come back the other way. At a median U-turn or J-turn intersection, the left turn is banned at the intersection itself, so drivers go through and make a U-turn at a median opening ahead.

lines.text: Tie: vehicle on the left yields.

narration.text: At an all-way stop the first vehicle to stop goes first. When two arrive together, the vehicle on the left yields, and if there is any doubt it is better to yield. Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise and enters or leaves only by right turns, and entering traffic always yields to traffic already circulating. A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, while a traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs on its approaches. So check which kind of circular intersection you are entering.

In a multi-lane roundabout, pick your lane before entering and do not change lanes while circulating. Yield to large vehicles going through the roundabout at the same time. When two large trucks are side by side, the one in the right lane yields to the one in the left lane. So in a roundabout with more than one lane, the lane choice happens before you enter, and large vehicles get the room they need. These rules add to the basic roundabout rule that entering traffic yields to circulating traffic. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Trap: all circles work the same.
Traffic circles may run both ways.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A circular intersection can be either a roundabout or a traffic circle, and they do not follow the same pattern. A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, entered and left only by right turns, with entering traffic yielding to circulating traffic. A traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs on its approaches. A second trap is the all-way stop tie. When two vehicles arrive together, the vehicle on the left yields, and if there is any doubt it is better to yield.

Here is a quick check: you are about to enter a roundabout and cars are already circulating. Who yields? Recall the roundabout rule. Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise and enters or leaves only by right turns, and entering traffic always yields to traffic already circulating. So the answer is that you yield. In a multi-lane roundabout you would also have picked your lane before entering, and you would yield to any large vehicle going through at the same time. If you thought circulating cars must make room for you, review the roundabout rule.

lines.text: Plan the lane early; signal with lights.
No U-turns on curves, crests, interstates.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Turn left from the far-left lane and right from the far-right lane, signal with your lights, and use hand signals only if a light fails, never on a skills exam. Never pass in a center left-turn lane. No U-turns on curves, near crests or on interstates, and at a median U-turn intersection go through and U-turn at a median opening. At an all-way stop, the first to stop goes first and the left vehicle yields in a tie. Roundabouts run counterclockwise with entering traffic yielding, lanes are chosen before entering, and the right-lane truck yields to the left-lane truck.

why_how.text: Speeding reduces steering ability, lengthens stopping distance and makes crashes more severe.
Indiana sets default limits by road type, and posted limits can be lower.

scenario.text: A driver in a passenger car is on a rural interstate with no lower limit posted.

reasoning.text: On rural interstates, passenger vehicles may not go over seventy miles per hour, and trucks over twenty-six thousand pounds may not go over sixty-five, or the lower posted limit.

result.text: The driver keeps to seventy or below, while a heavy truck on the same road keeps to sixty-five or below.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a work site speed limit applies only when workers are visible.

correction.text: A work site limit is always at least ten miles per hour below the area's normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply at all times.

memory_support.text: Seventy, sixty, fifty-five, thirty, fifteen; two to three seconds back.

prompt.text: What is the usual limit in an urban residential area unless another limit is posted?

rationale.text: Most urban residential areas have a thirty limit and alleys a fifteen limit unless another limit is posted.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on speed limits and following distance. In this lesson you will learn what going over the speed limit does to steering, stopping and crash severity, the default speed limits for rural interstates, rural divided highways, urban roads, residential areas and alleys, the special limits for school zones, work sites and school buses, how far behind the vehicle ahead you should stay, and what affects a vehicle's ability to stop. Many of these are numbers, so the lesson repeats each one as it goes. Keep this in mind as you practice.

Going over the speed limit reduces your ability to steer around curves and objects, lengthens emergency stopping distance and makes crashes more severe. Driving at or above the posted limit is even more dangerous in bad weather, on icy roads, with worn tires, with unsafe vehicle conditions or when physically impaired. So the posted limit is a maximum for good conditions, and each of those listed conditions makes driving at that speed more dangerous. These two facts explain why the rest of this lesson matters on every road type.

lines.text: Rural interstate: seventy; heavy trucks sixty-five.
Urban fifty-five; residential thirty; alleys fifteen.

narration.text: On rural interstates, passenger vehicles may not go over seventy miles per hour, and trucks with a declared gross weight over twenty-six thousand pounds may not go over sixty-five, or the lower posted limit. On a rural state divided highway, the limit is sixty or the posted limit. In urban areas of at least fifty thousand people, the limit is fifty-five on urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads unless a different limit is posted. Most urban residential areas have a thirty limit and alleys a fifteen limit unless another limit is posted.

title.text: School, work site and bus limits

lines.text: School zones: common weekday hours or beacons.
Work sites: at least ten lower.

narration.text: School zone limits commonly apply from seven a.m. to four thirty p.m. Monday through Friday or whenever the school beacons flash, and local authorities may set lower limits whenever children are present. A work site speed limit is always at least ten miles per hour below the area's normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply at all times. A school bus off interstates and state highways is limited to forty miles per hour, while on an interstate or highway its limit is sixty or the posted limit. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: About eighty point seven feet a second at fifty-five.

narration.text: Stay at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead, counting from when it passes a fixed object until you pass the same object. At fifty-five miles per hour a vehicle covers about eighty point seven feet each second, compared with about fifty-one point three feet at thirty-five and one hundred two point seven feet at seventy. Stopping ability depends on vehicle weight, brakes, tires, pavement condition and slickness, and the grade of the road. So the faster you go, the more ground you cover each second, and the gap ahead is your space to react and stop.

lines.text: Trap: work limits apply only with workers.
At least ten lower, flashing or always.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers slow down in a work site only when they see workers. The manual says a work site speed limit is always at least ten miles per hour below the area's normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply at all times. Another trap is mixing up limits. Seventy is for passenger vehicles on rural interstates, sixty for rural state divided highways, fifty-five for urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads, thirty for most residential areas and fifteen for alleys, unless another limit is posted.

Here is a quick check: what is the usual limit in an urban residential area unless another limit is posted? Go through the urban limits. Urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads have a fifty-five limit unless another is posted. Most urban residential areas have a thirty limit, and alleys have a fifteen limit, unless another limit is posted. So the answer is thirty miles per hour. If you chose fifty-five, remember that fifty-five belongs to the larger urban roads, not to residential streets. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Know the limit for the road.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Speeding reduces steering, lengthens stopping distance and makes crashes worse, especially in bad weather, on ice, with worn tires or when impaired. Default limits are seventy for cars and sixty-five for heavy trucks on rural interstates, sixty on rural divided highways, fifty-five on urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads, thirty in most residential areas and fifteen in alleys. School zones commonly apply on weekdays or when beacons flash, work sites are at least ten lower, and school buses are held to forty or sixty. Stay two to three seconds behind.

why_how.text: Skid recovery depends on your brakes, so the wrong technique can make a skid worse.
Rollovers make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths, and tire condition affects control.
If your vehicle runs off the road, do not jerk back onto the pavement; ease off the gas and steer back gradually.

scenario.text: Rae's car has anti-lock brakes, and she must stop hard on a slick road.

reasoning.text: With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer normally, without pumping, and pedal vibration or noise means ABS is working.

result.text: Rae holds firm pressure through the vibration and steers normally instead of pumping.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the skid technique depends on front-wheel or rear-wheel drive.

correction.text: The skid steps are the same for front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars; what changes the technique is whether the car has conventional or anti-lock brakes.

memory_support.text: Conventional: steer with the slide; anti-lock: press and steer, never pump.

prompt.text: Your car runs off the road onto the shoulder. What should you do?

answer.text: Ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe, without jerking back onto the pavement.

rationale.text: Overcorrecting is a common cause of rollovers, so you do not jerk back onto the pavement.

lines.text: Running off the road and rollovers.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on skids, rollovers, fuel and tires. In this lesson you will learn how to recover from a skid with conventional brakes and with anti-lock brakes, what to do if your vehicle runs off the road, what the manual says about rollover crashes and where they are more likely, how speed and short trips affect fuel use, and how to check tire pressure and tread depth. These topics are about keeping control of the car and keeping it in a condition that helps you stay in control. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Ease off the gas; do not oversteer.
Conventional: steer where the rear slides.
Anti-lock: press firmly, steer, no pumping.

narration.text: To recover from a skid, ease off the gas and avoid steering too far. With conventional brakes, steer smoothly in the direction the rear of the car is sliding. With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer normally, without pumping; pedal vibration or noise means ABS is working. The skid steps are the same for front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars. What changes the technique is whether the car has conventional or anti-lock brakes, so know which kind your car has before you need it.

lines.text: Do not jerk back onto the pavement.
Undivided roads and ditches raise the risk.

narration.text: If your vehicle runs off the road, do not jerk back onto the pavement. Ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe, since overcorrecting is a common cause of rollovers. Rollover crashes make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths. Keeping control of the vehicle is the biggest factor in avoiding one, and badly inflated or worn tires undermine that control. Rollovers are more likely on undivided two-way roads or divided roads without barriers, and a car leaving a rural road can roll when it hits a ditch, an embankment or soft soil.

lines.text: Check pressure cold; penny test for tread.

narration.text: Fuel use climbs steadily above forty-five miles per hour, and cars and light trucks use roughly fifty percent more fuel at seventy-five than at fifty-five. Several short trips from a cold start can burn twice as much fuel as one longer trip covering the same distance. Tires can lose up to one pound per square inch a month, so check pressure monthly or before a long trip, with tires cold, against the door-jamb sticker or owner's manual rather than the sidewall. In the penny test, if any part of Lincoln's head is covered by tread, you have a legal and safe amount.

lines.text: Trap: pump every brake in a skid.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers learn that pumping the brakes helps in a skid and apply that to every car. With anti-lock brakes, the manual says to keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer normally, without pumping, and that pedal vibration or noise means ABS is working. With conventional brakes, you ease off the gas and steer smoothly in the direction the rear of the car is sliding. A second trap is thinking front-wheel or rear-wheel drive changes the steps. It does not; the brake type does. Keep this in mind as you practice.

Here is a quick check: your car drifts off the road onto the shoulder. What should you do? Recall the run-off rule. Do not jerk back onto the pavement. Ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe, because overcorrecting is a common cause of rollovers. So the answer is to ease off the gas and steer back gradually. Rollover crashes make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths, and keeping control of the vehicle is the biggest factor in avoiding one. If you said to turn back sharply, review this rule.

lines.text: Steer with the slide or press firmly.
Ease back after leaving the road.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. In a skid, ease off the gas and do not oversteer; with conventional brakes steer where the rear slides, and with anti-lock brakes press firmly, steer normally and do not pump. Drive type does not change the steps. If you run off the road, ease off the gas and steer back gradually. Rollovers make up nearly one-third of passenger deaths, and control and good tires are key. Fuel use rises above forty-five and short cold trips burn more. Check tire pressure cold against the door-jamb sticker, and use the penny test for tread.

why_how.text: Ice, water, fog and darkness each call for specific actions from the driver.
Drowsiness and phones both take a driver's attention off the road.

scenario.text: A driver at night comes up behind another car on a dark road with high beams on.

reasoning.text: You must dim to low beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle or within two hundred feet behind another vehicle.

result.text: The driver switches to low beams before getting within two hundred feet of the car ahead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking high beams help you see better in fog.

correction.text: In fog, drive slowly with low beams rather than high beams, and if visibility drops to near zero, pull as far off the road as you can and stop.

memory_support.text: Low beams in fog; dim at five hundred facing, two hundred following.

prompt.text: Water covers the road ahead of you. What does the manual say to do?

answer.text: Never drive where water covers the road.

rationale.text: Never drive where water covers the road, and if your car stalls in a flooded area, leave it as soon as possible.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on weather, night driving and alertness. In this lesson you will learn which road surfaces freeze first, how to prepare for very cold weather, what to do about hydroplaning and wet brakes, how to handle flooded roads and fog, when headlights and low beams are required, how to avoid headlight glare, what the manual says about sleep loss and drowsy driving, and what Indiana law says about phones while driving. Each topic has a short list of actions to remember. Keep this in mind as you practice. Read each practice question carefully.

lines.text: Cold weather: warm up, full tank.

narration.text: Ramps, bridges and overpasses can freeze before the rest of the road, and drivers should keep a safe distance behind snowplows. In very cold weather, let the engine warm up, keep a full gas tank so the heater can run if you are stranded, and clear snow from headlights and taillights often. Hydroplaning gets worse as speed rises, and after driving through puddles, pump the brakes to dry them. So winter calls for watching the surfaces that freeze first and preparing the car, while rain calls for lower speeds and drying the brakes after deep puddles.

lines.text: Never drive where water covers the road.
Flash floods: the deadliest weather event.
Fog: low beams, slow, pull off if needed.

narration.text: Never drive where water covers the road, and if your car stalls in a flooded area, leave it as soon as possible. Flash flooding kills more people than any other roadway weather event each year, so never drive around barricades or past road closed signs. In fog, drive slowly with low beams rather than high beams, and if visibility drops to near zero, pull as far off the road as you can and stop. So water on the road and closed roads are reasons to turn back, and fog is a reason to slow down and use low beams. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Sunset to sunrise; under five hundred feet visibility.
Dim at five hundred facing, two hundred following.

narration.text: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and whenever visibility is under five hundred feet. You must dim to low beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle or within two hundred feet behind another vehicle. The low-beam rule uses five hundred feet for an oncoming vehicle but only two hundred feet when you are following another vehicle. To avoid the glare of oncoming headlights at night, do not look straight into them; focus on the right side of the road instead. So the two distances depend on whether the other car is coming toward you or ahead of you.

Studies cited in the manual say going eighteen hours without sleep impairs a driver as much as a point zero eight BAC, the legal alcohol limit. Young adults aged sixteen to twenty-nine are at the highest risk of drowsy driving, accounting for sixty-four percent of fatigue-related crashes. Warning signs include yawning or heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing exits, drifting onto rumble strips and failing to hold a steady speed. Indiana law bans using a telecommunications device while driving unless it is hands-free or you are calling nine-one-one in a real emergency, and a text takes your eyes off the road for five seconds.

Here are two traps about headlights. First, fog. It can seem that brighter lights will help, but the manual says to drive slowly with low beams rather than high beams in fog, and to pull as far off the road as you can and stop if visibility drops to near zero. Second, the low-beam distances. You dim within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle, but within two hundred feet when you are following another vehicle. Learners often use one number for both. Ask whether the other car is coming toward you or ahead of you. Keep this in mind as you practice.

Here is a quick check: water covers the road ahead of you. What does the manual say to do? Recall the flood rules. Never drive where water covers the road, and if your car stalls in a flooded area, leave it as soon as possible. Flash flooding kills more people than any other roadway weather event each year, so never drive around barricades or past road closed signs. So the answer is not to drive into the water. If you thought you could drive through slowly, review the flood rules in this lesson. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Bridges freeze first; dry brakes after puddles.
Never drive into water; low beams in fog.
Dim at five hundred or two hundred feet.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Ramps, bridges and overpasses can freeze first; keep back from snowplows, warm the engine and keep a full tank in very cold weather. Hydroplaning grows with speed, so pump the brakes after puddles. Never drive where water covers the road or around barricades, and leave a stalled car in a flood. In fog use low beams and slow down. Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and under five hundred feet of visibility; dim within five hundred feet facing and two hundred feet following, and look to the right edge. Watch for drowsiness, and use phones only hands-free or for an emergency call.

why_how.text: About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving.
Rural roads and interstates each have their own rules for speed, lights, lanes and stopping.
If you miss an interstate exit, drive on to the next one.

scenario.text: During one drive, a driver tailgates, fails to yield and honks without need.

reasoning.text: Under Indiana law, a driver is driving aggressively when at least three listed acts happen during one episode of continuous driving.

result.text: With three listed acts in one episode, this driver meets the definition of aggressive driving.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers already on the interstate must always let an entering car in.

correction.text: Drivers already on the interstate should make room, but entering drivers must yield to them.

memory_support.text: Three acts make aggression; missed exit, take the next.

prompt.text: You missed your exit on the interstate. What should you do?

answer.text: Drive on to the next exit.

rationale.text: Backing up is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on aggressive, rural and interstate driving. In this lesson you will learn what share of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving and what counts as dangerous driving, how Indiana law defines aggressive driving, how to handle gravel, dirt and hilly rural roads, and how to enter an interstate, what to do if you miss an exit, when you may stop on the shoulder, and which lanes trucks must use. Keep this in mind as you practice. Read each practice question carefully. Match the question to the exact rule.

lines.text: About one-third of deaths: dangerous driving.
Aggressive: three listed acts, one episode.

narration.text: About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, meaning crashes caused by aggressive driving, disregarding a signal or speeding. Under Indiana law, a driver is driving aggressively when at least three listed acts, such as tailgating, failure to yield or unnecessary horn use, happen during one episode of continuous driving. So dangerous driving is the wider group, which includes aggressive driving, disregarding a signal and speeding, and aggressive driving has its own legal test based on three listed acts in a single episode.

lines.text: Hill crests: slow, keep right, no passing.

narration.text: On gravel, traction is lower, so slow down earlier before turns and stops to avoid skidding. Before the crest of a steep hill, slow down, keep to the right and watch for oncoming vehicles, and never try to pass there. On dusty dirt roads, use low beam headlights so other drivers can see you. So each rural surface has one main adjustment: earlier braking on gravel, staying right and not passing near hill crests, and low beams in dust. These match the general rule that passing is illegal near the crest of a hill. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Missed exit: drive to the next.
Shoulders for emergencies; trucks keep right.

narration.text: When entering an interstate, stay right and build speed in the acceleration lane. Drivers already on the interstate should make room, but entering drivers must yield to them. If you miss an exit, drive on to the next one; backing up is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median. Do not stop or park on an interstate shoulder except for an emergency or a disabled vehicle. Trucks must stay in the right lane where an interstate has two lanes each way and in the right two lanes where it has three or more.

lines.text: Trap: interstate traffic must let you in.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because drivers on the interstate are expected to make room for entering traffic, some drivers merge as if they have the right of way. The manual says entering drivers must yield to vehicles already on the interstate, after building speed in the acceleration lane. A second trap is the missed exit. Backing up to reach a missed exit is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median. The answer is always to drive on to the next exit and come back. Keep this in mind as you practice.

Here is a quick check: you are on the interstate and you just missed your exit. What should you do? Recall the missed-exit rule. If you miss an exit, drive on to the next one. Backing up is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median. You also should not stop on the shoulder, which is only for an emergency or a disabled vehicle. So the answer is to drive on to the next exit. If you thought you could back up along the shoulder, review this rule. Keep this in mind as you practice.

lines.text: Slow early on gravel; no passing near crests.
Yield when entering; take the next exit.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, and aggressive driving means at least three listed acts in one episode. On gravel, slow down earlier; before a steep hill crest, slow down, keep right and never pass; on dusty dirt roads, use low beams. On the interstate, build speed in the acceleration lane and yield to traffic already there, take the next exit if you miss one, stop on the shoulder only for an emergency or a disabled vehicle, and expect trucks to keep to the right lanes.
